questions.question: Explain the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem with examples.
  • Biotic components of an ecosystem are all living things in the ecosystem, include
  • producers, consumers, and decomposers.
  •  Producers: Also known as autotroph, these organisms produce food through
  • photosynthesis. Eg: green plants and cyanobacteria.
  •  Consumers: Also known as heterotrophs, these organisms depend on other
  • autotrophs for food. Consumers are further classified into primary, secondary, tertiary
  • consumers. Eg: Tiger, elephant, human beings
  •  Decomposer: Also known as saprophytes, these organisms break down dead
  • and decaying organic matter into simpler molecules. Eg: fungi
  • The abiotic components of an ecosystem are the nonliving parts of the ecosystem
  • including air, water, soil, minerals, sunlight, temperature, nutrients, wind etc

questions.question: What is mean by hydrosphere? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is mean by hydrosphere? [K] / [CO1]
  • The hydrosphere is the total mass of water on Earth, encompassing all liquid, solid (ice), and gaseous (vapor)
  • water found on, under, and above the surface. It includes oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater, and
  • water vapor in the atmosphere, and it plays a crucial role in regulating climate and sustaining life.
  • Surface and underground water: This includes all bodies of water like oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers, as well
  • as groundwater and aquifers.
  • Frozen water: This component consists of ice sheets, glaciers, and snowcover.
  • Atmospheric water: This category includes water in the air as vapor and clouds.
  • Key role: The hydrosphere is vital for regulating Earth's climate and maintaining the balance of the Earth
  • system by influencing processes like the water cycle.

questions.question: Describe the characteristics of desert ecosystem. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the characteristics of desert ecosystem. [U] / [CO2]
  • Characteristics of desert ecosystem:
  • Climate and soil
  • Low precipitation: Deserts receive very little rainfall, typically less than 10 inches (250 mm)
  • per year.
  • Extreme temperatures: They experience large temperature swings between day and night. Days
  • can be scorching hot, while nights can become very cold.
  • High winds: High wind velocity is common, which can contribute to erosion and sand dunes.
  • Low humidity: The air holds very little moisture, which is why temperature regulations are so
  • extreme.
  • Soil: The soil is often sandy or rocky and can lack essential organic nutrients.
  • Vegetation and animal life
  • Sparse vegetation: Due to the scarcity of water, plant life is sparse and consists of drought-
  • tolerant species like cacti, succulents, and small shrubs.
  • Adapted organisms: Animals and plants have evolved specific adaptations to cope with the
  • harsh conditions. Examples include:
  • Water conservation: Animals develop physical traits to conserve water and plants have
  • mechanisms like deep root systems or waxy coatings.
  • Behavioral adaptations: Many animals are nocturnal to avoid the heat of the day.
  • Biodiversity: While life is challenging, deserts support a variety of life forms, including
  • insects, reptiles, and mammals, each with specialized survival traits.

questions.question: Point out the characteristics of grasslands / [CO2] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Point out the characteristics of grasslands [U] / [CO2]
  • Climate
  • Semi-arid conditions: Grasslands receive more rainfall than deserts but less than forests, typically between
  • 250 and 950 mm (10 to 37 inches) per year.
  • Seasonal variation: Temperate grasslands have cold winters and warm summers, while tropical grasslands
  • (savannas) have hot and wet seasons alternating with hot and dry seasons.
  • Prone to drought: The climate is often prone to periodic droughts and strong winds.
  • Vegetation
  • Grasses dominate: The defining characteristic is the dominance of grasses and other herbaceous plants.
  • Few trees: There are few trees, which are often limited to areas near rivers or streams.
  • Wildflowers: Wildflowers and shrubs are also common, especially during certain seasons.
  • Fire adaptations: Grasses are well-adapted to survive periodic wildfires, with deep roots that allow them to
  • regrow quickly after a fire.
  • Soil
  • Deep and fertile: The soil is often deep, dark, and rich in nutrients from the decomposition of dead plant
  • matter, making it ideal for farming.
  • Nutrient-dense: The constant cycle of grass dying back in winter or the dry season and regrowing contributes
  • to the soil's fertility.
  • Wildlife
  • Large herbivores: Grasslands support large grazing animals like bison, zebras, and elephants.
  • Predators: Carnivores such as lions, wolves, and cheetahs are also found in these ecosystems.
  • Small animals and birds: They are also home to numerous small mammals, such as prairie dogs and rabbits, as
  • well as various insects and birds.
  • Burrowing animals: Many grassland animals have adapted to the environment by burrowing to escape
  • predators, harsh weather, and fire.

questions.question: What is the nitrogen cycle? What are the steps involved in biological nitrogen fixation?
questions.solution_html:
• What is the nitrogen cycle? What are the steps involved in biological nitrogen
  • fixation.
  •  Nitrogen cycle is a biogeochemical process that moves nitrogen between the
  • atmosphere, land and living things.
  •  Most of the nitrogen in the earth atmosphere is in the form of nitrogen gas
  • (N2), which is not directly usable by living organisms.
  •  Nitrogen fixation: Bacteria or lightening convert nitrogen gas into ammonia,
  • a form of nitrogen that plant can use.
  •  Nitrification: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrates, which plant
  • can absorb.
  •  Denitrification: Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates and nitrites back into
  • nitrogen gas, which is released into the atmosphere.
  •  Ammonification: When plants and animals die, fungi break down their
  • remains into ammonia.
  •  The nitrogen cycle is essential for maintaining the balance of ecosystems.
  •  Human activities like using nitrogen fertilizers, burning fossil fuels, and
  • releasing nitrogen into waste water can alter the nitrogen cycle and harm the
  • environment and human health.

questions.question: What are the different types of aquatic ecosystems? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What are the different types of aquatic ecosystems? [U] / [CO1]
  • Aquatic ecosystems are broadly classified into freshwater, marine, and brackish water types based on
  • salinity. Freshwater ecosystems include still waters like lakes and ponds (lentic) and flowing waters like
  • rivers and streams (lotic). Marine ecosystems are salty oceans and seas, while brackish ecosystems are
  • where fresh and saltwater mix, such as estuaries and mangroves.
  • Freshwater ecosystems
  • Lentic: Still or slow-moving water bodies. Examples: Lakes, ponds, and some wetlands.
  • Lotic: Flowing or fast-moving water. Examples: Rivers, streams, and creeks.
  • Wetlands: Areas saturated with water, like marshes, swamps, and bogs.
  • Marine ecosystems
  • Salty water found in oceans, seas, and coastal areas. Examples: Open ocean, coral reefs, and coastal
  • zones.
  • Brackish water ecosystems
  • A mix of freshwater and saltwater. Examples: Estuaries, which are where rivers meet the sea, and
  • mangrove forests.

questions.question: Define Red data book. How it influence the biodiversity conservation? Explain. (1 × 10 = 10) END OF THE QUESTION PAPER ***
questions.solution_html:
• Define Red data book. How it influence the biodiversity conservation? Explain.
  •  Red data book is a public document that records endangered, rare, and
  • vulnerable species of plant, animal, and fungi.
  •  It is used to help identify and protect species that are at risk of extinction.
  •  The red data book was first issued by the special survival commission of the
  • IUCN IN 1964.
  •  The red data book uses colour coded information sheets to organize species by
  • their risk of extinction
  •  Black: Species that are confirmed extinct.
  •  Red: Species that are endangered
  •  Amber: Species that are vulnerable
  •  Green: Species that wear once endangered but are recovering
  •  White: Rare species
  •  Grey:Species that are vulnerable,endangered or rare, but there isn't enough
  • information to classify them
  •  The red data book classifies species into categories like threatened, not
  • threatened, and unknown.
  •  It also provide information on the population of particular species and helps to
  • estimate the risk of species becoming extinct.
  •  Red data book provides guidelines for protecting endangered species. (1X10=10)

questions.question: Describe Red data book. Explain its relevance. / [CO3] [1x10 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Red data book. Explain its relevance. [U] / [CO3]
  • A Red Data Book is a comprehensive public document that records and catalogs rare and endangered
  • species of plants, animals, and fungi. Its main purpose is to identify and safeguard species on the brink
  • of extinction to inform research and conservation efforts. The IUCN Red List is the most well-known
  • global version of this, which helps raise awareness and guides conservation strategies by providing data
  • on species' status and risks.
  • Relevance of the Red Data Book
  • Biodiversity conservation: It is crucial for biodiversity conservation as it provides valuable information
  • that can be used to develop policies and strategies for protecting vulnerable species.
  • Species identification: It helps identify which species are rare, at risk, or on the verge of extinction,
  • serving as a crucial resource for monitoring and research.
  • Conservation efforts: By documenting endangered species, it helps conservationists and researchers take
  • necessary actions to protect them.
  • Research and monitoring: It provides comprehensive data for research, studies, and monitoring
  • programs focused on rare and endangered species and their habitats.
  • International cooperation: It facilitates global cooperation in conservation efforts by providing a
  • common framework for assessing species risk and highlighting the need for concerted action.
  • Status assessment: The Red Data Book helps in evaluating the conservation status and risk of
  • endangerment for various species on a global scale.
  • Documentation of extinct species: The book includes a section with black pages to list species that are
  • already extinct, serving as a record of species that have been lost forever.
